one_line: chain-menu ranking tool for people on GLP-1 medication
skills: evidence review with explicit strength grading
SEO content architecture and PWA delivery
data: published chain nutrition information under the FDA menu-labeling rule (21 CFR 101.11), 15 chains
AHA added-sugar and sodium daily limits
GLP-1 body-composition and gastric-emptying literature cited in the rubric

decisions.chose: a categorical penalty for fried or breaded items that also caps the tier
decisions.over: letting fried items be handled by the fat-gram sub-score
decisions.because: a fried item can look moderate on the label and still trigger nausea
decisions.evidence: Fried is treated as a categorical penalty here (not just a fat-gram effect), because a fried item can carry moderate fat on the label yet still be a strong nausea trigger.

decisions.chose: shrinking the score toward a neutral 50 in proportion to missing nutrition fields
decisions.over: simply renormalizing over whichever fields happen to be present
decisions.because: otherwise one present field could carry an item to the top tier on almost no data
decisions.evidence: the normalized value is then shrunk toward a neutral 0.5 in proportion to how much of the 100-point signal is missing

decisions.chose: accepting total carbohydrates but not scoring them
decisions.over: adding a carbohydrate axis to catch refined starch
decisions.because: a direct carb penalty would punish high-carb, high-fiber items that suit the eating pattern
decisions.evidence: for now `carbs_g` is accepted but not scored on its own to avoid falsely penalizing legitimately high-carb, high-fiber items

decisions.chose: no calorie floor: small items are not penalized for being small
decisions.over: a symmetric portion score around an ideal calorie target
decisions.because: a small, protein-dense item is exactly what the GLP-1 eating pattern calls for
decisions.evidence: Note the asymmetry: a low-calorie item is not penalized for being small, because a small high-protein item is exactly what suits GLP-1 users

decisions.chose: a web app with a PWA install and Stripe planned for payments
decisions.over: shipping a native app through the App Store
decisions.because: it avoids the store cut and validates the idea faster
decisions.evidence: Freemium, web + Stripe first (keep 100 percent, no App Store cut, validate faster).

broke.what: the added-sugar axis cannot be scored as designed, because US chains publish total sugars only; the field carries total sugar as an upper bound and the compromise had to be documented on every item
broke.evidence: `sugarIsTotal: true` is set on every item, because U.S. restaurants publish **total sugars**, not added sugars.

broke.what: a chunk of the dataset could not be read off a single published item and had to be derived from per-ingredient values or comparable items, then flagged as estimated
broke.evidence: `estimated: true` marks any item whose numbers were derived rather than read off a single published SKU.

broke.what: the macro-consistency check fails on near-zero-calorie drinks, where the calories-from-macros ratio is meaningless
broke.evidence: The only large percentage gaps are on near-zero-calorie black coffees, where the ratio is not meaningful.

broke.what: the thresholds are not trial-backed, so the whole engine has to be presented as a ranking aid rather than a clinical instrument
broke.evidence: the nutrition guidance for people on GLP-1 receptor agonists ... is largely guidance-level and extrapolated from weight-loss physiology, dietitian practice, and drug mechanism, not from large randomized trials of specific menu-item macros

broke.what: refined starch slips through the scoring; white rice or white bread carries no added sugar and is only caught indirectly
broke.evidence: refined starch (for example white rice or white bread that carries no "added sugar") is only captured indirectly, through low fiber and low protein density

question: Can restaurant menu items be ranked transparently by how well they fit the way someone on a GLP-1 medication has to eat?
